'''Precious metals''' — gold, silver, platinum, palladium and copper — are tracked on MELEK by the [[KULA Community Fund|KULA]] account, which publishes a recurring market board. This article is the reference behind that board: what the numbers are, where they come from, and how to read them.

The board is drawn, not fetched as a picture. Every panel is generated from data constants in <code>integrations/metals-market.mjs</code> and emitted as plain SVG, so it is identical on every load and legible in print. No image model touches a number.

== The board ==

[[Figure:metals-board|Spot prices, the day's move, year to date, and where each metal sits inside its own yearly range.]]

Gold and silver are quoted to the cent from a bullion dealer's daily report and cross-checked against tokenised metal. Platinum, palladium and copper are consensus readings across several dealers, and the board labels them as such rather than inventing a daily tick for them. An approximate number labelled approximate is honest; an approximate number dressed up as a quote is not.

== 2026: a top, and a break ==

Both monetary metals made a high in 2026 and then fell hard. This is the single most important fact about the current market and the board leads with it.

[[Figure:metals-drawdown|How far gold and silver sit below their own 2026 peaks.]]

Gold peaked at $5,598.58 and trades about 27.7% below it. Silver peaked at $121.67 and trades about 55.7% below it — silver made the larger top and took the larger fall, which is what silver characteristically does. Silver's higher volatility is not a defect of the metal; it follows from a much smaller market in which industrial and speculative demand sit on top of the monetary bid.

== The ratio ==

[[Figure:gold-silver-ratio|The gold/silver ratio: how many ounces of silver one ounce of gold buys.]]

See [[The Gold-Silver Ratio]].

== Where silver goes ==

[[Figure:silver-demand|Silver demand by end use, 2026 forecast, and the annual supply deficit.]]

Silver is unusual among the precious metals in that most of it is *consumed*. Industrial fabrication is about 58% of demand — solar cells, electrical contacts, brazing alloys, vehicle electronics and data-centre hardware. Gold, by contrast, is overwhelmingly hoarded: almost every ounce ever mined still exists.

[[Figure:silver-demand-change|What grew and what collapsed in silver demand, by end use.]]

The market has run an annual supply deficit for six consecutive years. A deficit is drawn down from above-ground stocks rather than from the mine, so it can persist for years without forcing the price — which is why a deficit is a condition, not a signal.

== The long view ==

[[Figure:metals-history|Sixty-six years of gold, silver and platinum, on a logarithmic axis.]]

The axis is logarithmic deliberately. Gold went from about $35 to over $4,000, a range of more than a hundred times; on a linear axis the first thirty years are crushed into a flat line and the chart misrepresents them. On a log axis equal vertical distance is equal *percentage* change, which is what a holder actually experiences, so the 1970s and the 2020s can be compared honestly.

[[Figure:metals-decades|Returns by decade, as a total and as the same change expressed per year.]]

The decade table is computed from the series rather than typed in, so it cannot drift away from the chart above it.

== Reading the board honestly ==

Three habits the board is built to enforce:

* '''A price is a reading, not a forecast.''' The board shows what the metal costs and what it has done. It does not tell anyone what to buy. That is out of scope — see the note on individualised financial advice in the project's scope rules.
* '''Label precision.''' Numbers verified to the cent are shown to the cent; consensus readings are marked as consensus.
* '''Show the shape, not the story you want.''' Where the data is volatile rather than trending, the chart says so. See [[Silverware]] for the clearest case.
